subtitle: How a Jain Scholar Turned Subtle Numbers into Everyday Tools

panels.shot: low-angle mid-wide of a scholar in a pillared Jain temple hall, palm-leaf manuscript in hand, numbers and geometric forms sketched on the floor around him
panels.action: Mahāvīrācārya stands calm yet intense in a stone-pillared hall, palm-leaf bundle in one hand and a stylus in the other, surrounded by neatly traced circles, triangles and place-value numbers on a sanded floor.

dialogue.text: In 9th‑century Karnataka, as kings fought for land, a Jain mathematician named Mahāvīrācārya quietly forged a handbook that made subtle numbers serve merchants, builders and thinkers for a thousand years.

i18n.hi: नवीं सदी के कर्नाटक में, जब राजा ज़मीन के लिए लड़ रहे थे, जैन गणितज्ञ महावीराचार्य ने चुपचाप ऐसा ग्रंथ गढ़ा जिसने सूक्ष्म अंकों को हज़ार साल तक बनियों, मिस्त्रियों और विद्वानों की सेवा में लगा दिया।

panels.shot: bird’s-eye wide over the Deccan landscape, showing hilltop Jain temples and distant fortified cities under a hazy sky
panels.action: From high above, the rugged Deccan plateau stretches away with scattered towns, a hill crowned by a Jain temple, and in the distance the walls of a Rashtrakuta city catching the evening light.

dialogue.text: Around 850 CE, the Deccan shook under Rashtrakuta and Ganga rivalries, yet between their courts Jain scholars in Karnataka moved freely, carrying not swords but palm leaves filled with numbers.

i18n.hi: लगभग 850 ईस्वी में, दक्खिन पर राष्ट्रकूट और गंगा की टक्कर गूँज रही थी, पर उनके दरबारों के बीच कर्नाटक के जैन विद्वान बिना तलवार, सिर्फ़ अंकों से भरी ताड़‑पत्तों की पोटलियाँ लेकर आते‑जाते रहे।

panels.shot: slow push-in on Mahāvīrācārya seated cross-legged in a quiet Jain temple cloister, manuscripts spread before him
panels.action: Mahāvīrācārya sits cross‑legged in a shaded cloister, robes simple, his shaved head bowed over a spread of palm‑leaf manuscripts, thin stylus poised while faint chanting drifts from the shrine beyond.

dialogue.text: Mahāvīrācārya was a Jain scholar, likely under King Amoghavarsha’s Rashtrakuta shadow, drawing on older works like Āryabhaṭa and Bhāskara I, yet restless to tighten and arrange their scattered rules.

i18n.hi: महावीराचार्य जैन आचार्य थे, शायद राष्ट्रकूट राजा अमोघवर्ष के साये में, आर्यभट और भास्कर प्रथम जैसे पुराने ग्रंथों से सीखते हुए, पर उनके बिखरे नियमों को कड़ा कर के क्रम में बाँधने को बेचैन।

panels.shot: medium close-up on Mahāvīrācārya’s hands as he copies and annotates an older manuscript
panels.action: A close view shows Mahāvīrācārya’s careful hands aligning a brittle old leaf beside a fresh one, inscribing neat lines while adding small marginal marks, his face intent in the lamplight.

dialogue.text: The older Sanskrit verses gave rules for sines, circles, progressions and place‑value. Mahāvīra’s question was sharp: how can this living stream of ganita be organised so anyone trained may drink from it?

i18n.hi: पुरानी संस्कृत पंक्तियाँ ज्या, वृत्त, समान्तर श्रेणी और स्थान‑मान की विधियाँ देती थीं। महावीर का सवाल नुकीला था: इस जीवित गणित धारा को कैसे सहेजें कि कोई भी प्रशिक्षित व्यक्ति खुल कर पी सके?

panels.shot: wide interior shot of a Jain temple school, with young students, an abacus-like counting board, and merchants observing
panels.action: In a long hall, students sit in rows before sand boards and shell counters, while two visiting merchants in turbans watch as a teacher traces columns of digits and miniature granaries on the floor.

dialogue.text: In Karnataka’s Jain schools, commerce pressed on theory. Grain dealers, land stewards and temple builders needed clear methods for shares, depths, volumes, interest and partitions, not only sky‑circles and stars.

i18n.hi: कर्नाटक की जैन पाठशालाओं में व्यापार ने सिद्धांत को धक्का दिया। अनाज़ व्यापारी, ज़मींदार और मंदिर‑निर्माता को हिस्सों, गहराइयों, घनफल, ब्याज और बँटवारे के साफ़ तरीके चाहिए थे, सिर्फ़ आकाश‑वृत्त और तारों के नहीं।

panels.shot: extreme close-up on Mahāvīrācārya’s face, eyes reflecting rows of numbers and geometric figures
panels.action: Mahāvīrācārya looks up from his work, eyes bright, as ghostly reflections of place‑value digits and simple diagrams seem to float in the darkness before him.

dialogue.text: Mahāvīrācārya’s answer took the form of a single text in simple metrical Sanskrit, the Gaṇita‑Sāra‑Saṅgraha—‘Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics’—that marched from basic numeration through geometry to combinations.

i18n.hi: महावीराचार्य ने समाधान एक ही ग्रंथ में दिया, सरल छंदों वाली संस्कृत में—‘गणित‑सार‑संग्रह’—जो मूल अंकगणना से चल कर ज्यामिति और संयोग‑क्रमचय तक सीधी रेखा में बढ़ता है।

panels.shot: tabletop overhead shot of a palm-leaf colophon page being inscribed with the title and chapter divisions
panels.action: From above, a fresh palm leaf shows ruled lines as Mahāvīrācārya incises the opening verses, with simple symbols marking sections on numbers, fractions, measures, series and mixed problems.

dialogue.text: He set his work in nine chapters: on numbers, the basic operations, fractions, mixed fractions, series, geometry and mensuration, shadows, combinations and permutations, and a closing garland of practical tasks.

i18n.hi: उन्होंने इसे नौ अध्यायों में बाँधा: संख्याएँ, चार मूल क्रियाएँ, भिन्न, मिश्र भिन्न, श्रेणियाँ, ज्यामिति और क्षेत्रफल‑घनफल, छाया, संयोग‑क्रमचय, और अंत में व्यावहारिक प्रश्नों की एक माला।

panels.shot: medium shot of Mahāvīrācārya teaching two students using a dust board, writing 0 within a larger numeral
panels.action: Before two attentive students, Mahāvīrācārya squats at a dust board, calmly writing place‑value numerals with a small circle for emptiness between digits as he explains with his free hand raised.

dialogue.text: Older Indian texts had already used empty places and a dot for zero; Mahāvīra firmly gave zero its seat among numbers, treating it in addition, subtraction, multiplication and division like any other digit.

i18n.hi: पुराने भारतीय ग्रंथ खाली स्थान और शून्य के लिए बिंदु जानते थे; महावीर ने शून्य को अंकों की पंक्ति में पक्का आसन दिया, उसे जोड़, घटाव, गुणा, भाग में किसी और अंक जैसा ही साधा।

panels.shot: close-up of the dust board showing Mahāvīrācārya writing a small circle and demonstrating an operation
panels.action: A close view shows his stylus shaping a small circle and placing it between digits as he gestures to show its role in forming a larger number on the smooth dust surface.

dialogue.speaker: mahaviracharya
dialogue.text: Where nothing is, we place a sign; where nothing stands, the count still flows.

i18n.hi: जहाँ कुछ नहीं, वहाँ चिह्न रखते हैं; जहाँ कुछ नहीं खड़ा, वहाँ भी गिनती चलती रहती है।

panels.shot: medium-wide of Mahāvīrācārya guiding a student through a fraction problem with a merchant listening nearby
panels.action: Mahāvīrācārya kneels beside a young student who scratches fraction bars and numerators in the sand, while a bearded merchant leans forward, intrigued, a cloth bag of coins resting by his knee.

dialogue.text: He worked out clear rules for fractions—reducing, comparing, adding and subtracting shares—framing them in verses about dividing fields, barrels of ghee, and partnership profits so that reciters could remember and apply.

i18n.hi: उन्होंने भिन्नों के साफ़ नियम गढ़े—सरलीकरण, तुलना, जोड़‑घटाव—और उन्हें खेत बाँटने, घी के मटके और साझेदारी के लाभ की कविताओं में पिरोया, ताकि गाने वाले याद रखें और लागू कर सकें।

panels.shot: wide shot of a courtyard where builders measure a rectangular foundation while Mahāvīrācārya watches
panels.action: In a sunlit courtyard, masons stretch cords along a rectangular foundation while Mahāvīrācārya stands nearby, tracing a rectangle and triangle on a tablet, indicating how to compute area and height.

dialogue.text: The Gaṇita‑Sāra‑Saṅgraha gathered area and volume rules for rectangles, triangles, circles, heaps and tanks, echoing older śulba and astronomical texts but polishing them into one ready handbook for craftsmen and scribes.

i18n.hi: गणित‑सार‑संग्रह ने आयत, त्रिकोण, वृत्त, ढेर और तालाब के क्षेत्रफल‑घनफल के नियम एक जगह समेटे, पुराने शुल्ब‑सूत्र और खगोलीय ग्रंथों की गूँज रखते हुए भी उन्हें कारीगरों और लेखकों के लिए एक तैयार हस्तपुस्तिका बना दिया।

panels.shot: medium shot of Mahāvīrācārya drawing a circle and inscribing a polygon inside it on a board
panels.action: Mahāvīrācārya draws a large circle on a wooden board and then inscribes a neat polygon within it, pausing to point at the chord while a student peers closely.

dialogue.text: Geometry in his verse dealt with chords, circles and polygons in the practical Indian fashion—rules for circumferences, chord lengths and areas—without proof diagrams, yet precise enough for architecture and land survey.

i18n.hi: उनकी ज्यामिति‑कविता भारतीय ढंग से जीवा, वृत्त और बहुभुज सँभालती है—परिधि, जीवा‑लंबाई और क्षेत्रफल के नियमों से—बिना प्रमाण‑चित्रों के, पर वास्तु और नाप‑जोख के लिए काफी सटीक।

panels.shot: close-up of a palm-leaf where a problem verse about combinations is being written, showing arrangements of syllables as tiny marks
panels.action: The tip of his stylus presses into a leaf as he writes a verse, beside which tiny dots and lines mark different ways objects can be arranged in order and in groups.

dialogue.text: Most striking were his chapters on combinations and permutations—counting ways to arrange and choose objects—building on a long Indian taste for prosody and arrangements, now turned into general rules for ordered selections.

i18n.hi: सबसे चौंकाने वाले उनके संयोग और क्रमचय के अध्याय थे—वस्तुओं को चुनने और सजाने के तरीकों की गिनती—जो छंद‑रचना और विन्यास की पुरानी भारतीय रुचि को अब क्रमित चयन के सामान्य नियमों में बदल देते हैं।

panels.shot: medium shot of Mahāvīrācārya explaining a combinations problem about garlands or jewels to a noble patron
panels.action: In a modest court chamber, Mahāvīrācārya faces a seated noble, illustrating different possible arrangements of colored gems on a string using pebbles laid out in distinct orders.

dialogue.speaker: mahaviracharya
dialogue.text: Change the order, and the count grows. Fix the order, and the count falls.

i18n.hi: क्रम बदलो, तरीकों की गिनती बढ़ती है; क्रम बाँध दो, गिनती घट जाती है।

panels.shot: wide shot of a dim hall where Mahāvīrācārya dictates while a group of scribes copy his text onto fresh palm leaves
panels.action: In a long, lamp‑lit hall, Mahāvīrācārya sits at the head, reciting measured verses while several young scribes, each with palm leaves and stylus, copy his words in unison rows.

dialogue.text: He cast his rules as terse verses easy to chant, then oversaw copies for far monasteries and schools, turning his own memory into a thing that could travel, be recited, checked and corrected.

i18n.hi: उन्होंने नियमों को छोटे, गाए जा सकने वाले श्लोकों में बाँधा, फिर दूर‑दराज़ विहारों और पाठशालाओं के लिए प्रतिलिपियाँ बनवाईं, ताकि अपनी स्मृति को चलने‑फिरने, सुनने‑सुनाने, जाँचने‑सँवारने लायक बना सकें।

panels.shot: montage-like wide showing different users: a merchant tallying, a land surveyor, a temple accountant, all with manuscripts referencing similar diagrams
panels.action: A layered scene shows a merchant counting sacks with a leaf by his side, a land surveyor measuring fields with rope, and a temple accountant marking interest on a tablet—each with a manuscript showing similar neat figures.

dialogue.text: Over time, his compendium joined the working library of merchants, accountants, land‑record keepers and teachers, who found in it a consistent path from simple counting into shares, interest, measures and rarer puzzles.

i18n.hi: धीरे‑धीरे उनका संग्रह व्यापारियों, मुनीमों, भू‑अभिलेखकारों और आचार्यों की कामकाजी लाइब्रेरी में शामिल हुआ, जहाँ उन्हें साधी हुई राह मिली—साधारण गिनती से लेकर हिस्सों, ब्याज, माप और अनोखी पहेलियों तक।

panels.shot: medium shot of a later medieval mathematician reading Mahāvīrācārya’s text alongside a newer manuscript, in a different script
panels.action: Centuries later, another scholar in a different script and dress bends over an old palm leaf of Mahāvīrācārya’s work laid beside his own newer manuscript, marking notes and corrections along its margin.

dialogue.text: Later mathematicians like Bhāskara II met Mahāvīra as one voice among many, sometimes praising, sometimes correcting his rules, yet still copying his problems and structure into their own broader treasuries of ganita.

i18n.hi: भास्कर द्वितीय जैसे बाद के गणितज्ञों ने महावीर को कई आवाज़ों में से एक माना—कहीं प्रशंसा, कहीं संशोधन—पर फिर भी उनके प्रश्नों और ढाँचे को अपने विस्तृत गणित‑ग्रंथों में उठा कर जोड़ा।

panels.shot: wide shot of Shravanabelagola hill with a Jain temple, juxtaposed with faint overlay of numerical verses in the sky
panels.action: The hill of Śravaṇabelagola rises with its Jain temple silhouetted, while faint lines of numerical verse and simple digits seem to hover above the landscape like thin clouds.

dialogue.text: The same Jain networks that carved stone colossi at places like Śravaṇabelagola also quietly fostered such mathematical texts, tying the stillness of their hills to the restless movement of accounts and measures.

i18n.hi: जिन जैन जालों ने श्रवणबेलगोला जैसे स्थलों पर पत्थर के महाकाय प्रतिमान गढ़े, उन्होंने चुपचाप ऐसे गणित‑ग्रंथ भी पाले, अपनी शांत पहाड़ियों को खाते‑किताब और नाप‑तौल की बेचैन हलचलों से जोड़ते हुए।

panels.shot: slow pull-back from a close-up of the Gaṇita-Sāra-Saṅgraha manuscript to a shelf of many later works, while faint sounds of old courts fade
panels.action: A close view of a Gaṇita‑Sāra‑Saṅgraha manuscript slowly pulls back to reveal it resting among many later works on a shelf, while beyond, the vague outline of an old court fades into shadow.

dialogue.text: Mahāvīrācārya did not invent zero or algebra, but by gathering old currents into one ordered stream, he made numbers clear enough to outlast the Rashtrakuta courts that once sheltered his quiet labour.

i18n.hi: महावीराचार्य ने न शून्य गढ़ा, न बीजगणित, पर पुरानी धाराओं को एक सधे हुए प्रवाह में समेट कर उन्होंने अंकों को इतना साफ़ बना दिया कि वे उन राष्ट्रकूट दरबारों से भी अधिक टिके रहे जिन्होंने कभी उनके शांत श्रम को आसरा दिया था।

title_i18n.hi: महावीर ने गणना को काम की बना दिया

subtitle_i18n.en: How a Jain Scholar Turned Subtle Numbers into Everyday Tools
subtitle_i18n.hi: जैन आचार्य ने सूक्ष्म अंकों को रोज़ के औज़ार कैसे बनाया
